cim: Artificial intelligence and intellectual property rights: the situation in Thailand
cim_eredeti: Artificial intelligence and intellectual property rights: the situation in Thailand
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is transforming how businesses innovate, create content and commercialise intellectual assets. While AI offers significant opportunities, it challenges legal concepts developed around human creators and inventors, raising complex questions regarding ownership, infringement and protection.

AI can be both a creator and consumer of intellectual property (IP). AI systems are trained using vast quantities of potentially copyrighted data, while their outputs may resemble existing works or generate content that would traditionally qualify for IP protection if created by a human. Simultaneously, AI technologies themselves represent valuable commercial assets that businesses seek to protect. These overlapping roles have exposed gaps in legal frameworks worldwide.

Thailand’s current IP framework predates modern AI and provides limited guidance on AI-generated works, AI training practices and AI-generated inventions. This article reviews the existing legal framework, explores key IP issues arising from AI and discusses practical considerations and future developments.

Thailand currently has no AI-related IP laws. Existing legal principles generally apply to AI-related activities, but there is limited guidance on AI model training, no text and data-mining exceptions and little judicial precedent that could be applied to AI- and IP-related legal issues.

This position is broadly consistent with the wider Southeast Asian landscape, where copyright protection remains closely linked to human authorship and legislation is largely silent on AI-generated content. As a result, AI developers, organisations deploying third-party AI tools, content creators using generative AI and investors assessing AI-related legal risks must rely on contractual relationships to ensure legitimate use and mitigate legal exposure. The absence of clear AI-specific rules elevates the importance of contracts and internal governance, making contractual arrangements the primary mechanism for allocating ownership, liability and risk. Businesses should consider legal protections early on in the AI adoption process rather than waiting for regulatory certainty.

Regarding IP disputes, Thailand’s Civil Court issued a regulation, effective since 17 November 2025, governing the use of AI in the preparation of pleadings and other documents submitted to the court. The Civil Court’s rule is consistent with guidance previously issued by the President of the Supreme Court in September 2025, which was intended to promote accuracy, transparency and public confidence in the administration of justice. The Civil Court’s rules require parties and their counsel to disclose any AI-generated content submitted to the Civil Court and to verify and certify its accuracy. IP cases in Thailand must be filed at a specialised court called the Central IP and International Trade Court (IP&IT Court). It is likely that the IP&IT Court will issue similar rules related to the use of AI, but as of the date of this article, no such announcement has been made.

Among all of the available IP protections, copyright presents the most significant challenges for AI developers, users and content creators.

Copyright law in Thailand, as in many jurisdictions, is founded on human authorship. While the law protects original literary, artistic, musical, audiovisual and software works, it does not expressly address works generated autonomously by AI systems.

International developments point in a similar direction. The US Copyright Office has confirmed that copyright protection generally requires human authorship, while acknowledging that AI-assisted works may qualify where sufficient human creative contribution exists. Although not binding in Thailand, this provides a useful indication that it is very likely that Thai regulators and Thai courts may adopt a similar approach.

For businesses and creators, human involvement in the creative process should be carefully documented. Records demonstrating how individuals selected, arranged, modified or contributed to AI-generated content may become important for establishing ownership or enforcing copyright claims.

Even where sufficient human involvement supports a copyright claim, ownership may not be straightforward. Questions may arise as to whether rights belong to the individual user, the organisation directing the project, the employer or another party. Contractual arrangements can resolve many of these issues, but businesses should review ownership provisions carefully before relying on AI-generated content commercially. For example, under Section 9 of the Thai Copyright Act B.E. 2537 (1994), the default rule is that an employee owns the copyright in a work created in the course of employment, unless the parties have agreed otherwise in writing. Therefore, businesses must ensure that employment agreements adequately address the ownership of copyright works created using AI tools.

A more pressing issue concerns using copyrighted material to train AI models. Modern AI systems depend on vast datasets containing text, images, code, audio, video and other content, much of which may be protected by copyright.

Unlike Singapore and Japan, Thailand does not provide a broad text- and data-mining exception permitting the use of copyrighted works for AI training purposes. Reproducing copyrighted works to train AI models may constitute infringement unless authorisation has been obtained or a specific statutory exception applies.

This creates significant challenges. Rights clearance at scale is time-consuming, expensive and sometimes impossible. The lack of clear legislative guidance creates uncertainty, exposing developers to potential infringement claims, injunctions and damages.

Developers may also face allegations that model outputs reproduce protected content or constitute unauthorised derivative works. Although these questions remain largely unresolved under Thai law, they are increasingly subject to litigation elsewhere and such approaches are likely to influence future discussions in Thailand.

Data scraping presents additional issues. Publicly accessible information cannot necessarily be copied into training datasets without legal consequences. Businesses should not assume publicly available content is automatically available for AI training, as most such content is protected under copyright law in most jurisdictions and requires explicit consent for use, particularly for commercial purposes.

Given these risks, businesses should undertake careful due diligence concerning training data origins, terms governing third-party AI tools and the licensing status of materials used in model development. Organisations should review whether AI vendors use customer inputs for model training, which rights users retain in regard to any outputs and whether indemnities are available for infringement claims.

Companies commissioning customised AI solutions should seek contractual protection, including warranties regarding training data sources and indemnities for IP infringement. Robust contractual drafting remains one of the most important risk-management tools available.

Patents remain important for protecting AI innovation. Novel processes, technical applications, system architectures and implementation methods may be eligible for patent protection if they satisfy the relevant novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability requirements.

However, AI-related applications often encounter challenges because mathematical methods and abstract ideas are generally not patentable. Applicants are more likely to obtain protection where an AI innovation connects to a specific technical application, such as medical diagnosis, industrial automation, logistics management or fraud detection, rather than the underlying algorithm alone.
